topics.title: History and symptoms
topics.summary: From Dr Sheppard's week 8 lecture and seminar: the history is the most important part of the eye examination (over 70% of diagnoses can come from it). Take it in a logical order, follow up every symptom with LOFTSEA, ask everyone the standard symptom check, and record negatives.
keyPoints: Ask permission to take the history; show empathy, listen actively, keep open body language and don't interrupt. Patients' uninterrupted talking time is usually 30 seconds to a minute.
General observation matters: appearance, head posture, facial asymmetry, lids, eyes, speech and emotional state; age, sex and ethnicity change the likelihood of some conditions.
Reason for visit: open with 'Is there any particular reason for your visit today?' and record it in the patient's words. Return to it at the end.

LOFTSEA: Location, Onset (sudden can mean serious), Frequency, Type and severity, Self-treatment, Effect on the patient, Associated symptoms. Visual problems tend to come with eye use, on weekdays, building through the day.
Ask everyone about distance and near vision, eyestrain, headaches, pain or burning, diplopia, and flashes and floaters (especially high myopes).
Ocular history: each pair of spectacles, contact lens wear and care, low vision aids, past injuries, infections, surgery or patching, and the last eye exam.

General health: ask specifically about high blood pressure and diabetes (how long, last check), medication (including drops, hay fever and contraceptive pills; check the BNF) and allergies or reactions to drops.
Family history: strabismus, glaucoma, hypertension and diabetes. Lifestyle: occupation, sport, hobbies, driving and smoking (the strongest environmental risk factor for AMD).
Suggested order: general information, last eye exam, reason for visit, ocular history, family ocular history, general health, family medical history, symptom check, occupation and lifestyle.
Record in pen, legibly and fully, including negatives (no record means not asked), using only accepted abbreviations.
examTraps: Accepting 'double vision' at face value: ask if they see two of everything and whether it goes with one eye closed.
Not following up a headache because the patient says it isn't their eyes.
Assuming old records are still current.

diagram.description: A funnel: wide at the top with open questions (reason for visit), narrowing through symptom details, ocular history, general health and medication, family history, and lifestyle, ending in a short list of hypotheses at the bottom.

goDeeper.heading: Symptom clues
goDeeper.body: Constant distance blur: myopia, or nuclear sclerosis in older people. Intermittent: young diabetics, pseudomyopia. Near blur fine in good light: presbyopia. Both: astigmatism or pathology. Visual headaches are mild to moderate, dull, above or behind the eyes and linked to eye use. Pain or burning often means dry eye. Diplopia that persists with one eye closed is monocular (cataract, irregular astigmatism); pathological or traumatic diplopia is more often vertical.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: SOCRATES and red flags
goDeeper.body: For pain, SOCRATES (site, onset, character, radiation, associations, time course, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity) is another framework. Red flags include sudden vision loss, flashes with a curtain, a painful red eye, new diplopia, and headache with visual or neurological symptoms.

topics.title: Building a differential diagnosis
topics.summary: A differential diagnosis is a ranked list of what could explain the findings. Rank by likelihood, but always include the conditions you can't afford to miss, then choose tests that separate them.
keyPoints: List possibilities from the key symptom and sign (e.g. 'sudden painless loss of vision in one eye').
Think anatomically (front to back) and by mechanism (vascular, inflammatory, infective, degenerative, neoplastic, traumatic).
Rank by likelihood (age, history, risk factors) and by seriousness.
Always keep 'can't miss' diagnoses on the list until ruled out (e.g. retinal detachment, GCA, angle closure).
Choose discriminating tests: pupils (RAPD), IOP, fields, staining, dilated fundus exam.
Revisit the list as new results come in.
Management follows from the most likely and most serious possibilities.
examTraps: Stopping at the first diagnosis that fits ('premature closure').
Ranking only by likelihood and forgetting serious but rarer causes.
Doing every test instead of the ones that discriminate.

cases.scenario: A 66-year-old with hypertension noticed sudden painless blurring in the right eye this morning. VA R 6/36, L 6/6. Fundus: widespread flame haemorrhages in all four quadrants of the right eye with dilated tortuous veins.
cases.question: What's your differential and plan?

topics.title: Diabetes and the eye
topics.summary: Diabetic retinopathy is a microvascular disease graded in England by the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme (R0–R3, M0–M1). Diabetes also affects refraction, the lens, cranial nerves and the cornea. Know the signs in order of severity and the referral rules.
keyPoints: Earliest sign: microaneurysms. Then dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots.
Pre-proliferative (R2): venous beading or reduplication, IRMA, multiple deep blot haemorrhages.
Proliferative (R3A): new vessels (on the disc or elsewhere), pre-retinal or vitreous haemorrhage, fibrosis.
Maculopathy (M1): exudate within 1 disc diameter of the fovea, a group of exudates in the macula, or haemorrhage/MA near the fovea with reduced VA.
Risk factors for progression: duration, poor glucose control (HbA1c), high blood pressure, raised lipids, pregnancy, rapid improvement in control.
Other effects: refraction shifts with blood sugar changes, earlier cataract, cranial nerve palsies (III often pupil-sparing), reduced corneal sensation, rubeosis and neovascular glaucoma.
Everyone with diabetes aged 12+ should attend annual DESP screening (intervals are being extended for some low-risk people).
examTraps: Confusing hard exudates (yellow, well-defined) with cotton wool spots (white, fluffy).
Calling cotton wool spots alone 'proliferative'.
Prescribing glasses during a period of unstable blood sugar.

diagram.description: Fundus drawing showing: microaneurysms (tiny red dots), blot haemorrhages, hard exudates (yellow, near the macula), cotton wool spots (white fluffy), venous beading, IRMA, and new vessels at the disc (NVD) and elsewhere (NVE).

goDeeper.heading: DESP grading in brief
goDeeper.body: R0 none; R1 background (MAs, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots with other non-referable features); R2 pre-proliferative (venous beading/loop/reduplication, IRMA, multiple deep round or blot haemorrhages); R3A active proliferative; R3S stable treated proliferative. M0 no maculopathy; M1 maculopathy. U = ungradable. R3A is referred urgently; R2 and M1 are referred to the hospital eye service. Check the current DESP grading definitions.

goDeeper.heading: Diabetes and refraction
goDeeper.body: High blood glucose can change the lens's refractive index and hydration, often causing a myopic shift; as control improves the refraction moves back. If someone has been recently diagnosed or their control has just changed, it's often wise to delay a new prescription until blood sugar is stable, explaining why.

goDeeper.heading: Optometrist's role
goDeeper.body: Check that patients with diabetes are attending DESP, examine the fundus (dilated where appropriate), recognise sight-threatening signs between screenings and refer accordingly, and give lifestyle messages: blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, attending screening.

topics.title: Hypertension and the eye
topics.summary: High blood pressure damages retinal vessels over time (narrowing, AV nipping, wiring) and acutely in severe hypertension (haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, exudates, disc swelling). It also raises the risk of vein and artery occlusions.
keyPoints: Chronic changes: generalised and focal arteriolar narrowing, AV nipping, copper or silver wiring (arteriosclerosis).
Acute/severe changes: flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates (sometimes a macular star), disc swelling.
Classifications: Keith–Wagener–Barker (grades 1–4) or the simpler Wong–Mitchell (mild, moderate, malignant).
Hypertension raises the risk of branch and central retinal vein occlusion, artery occlusion and ischaemic optic neuropathy.
NICE NG136: clinic BP of 180/120 mmHg or more with retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema needs same-day specialist assessment.
Measuring BP in practice (where trained and equipped) can support appropriate referral.
Often asymptomatic — your fundus findings may be the first clue.
examTraps: Missing bilateral disc swelling in a patient with very high BP (accelerated hypertension).
Calling AV nipping 'normal crossings'.
Forgetting to check BP and refer when you see hypertensive signs.

diagram.description: Close-up of an artery crossing over a vein. Normal crossing: vein continuous. AV nipping: vein appears narrowed/hidden either side of the artery and deflected. Copper wiring: artery with a broad orange light reflex; silver wiring: artery appears white.

goDeeper.heading: Wong–Mitchell classification
goDeeper.body: Mild: generalised or focal arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, opacity ('wiring') of arteriolar walls. Moderate: haemorrhages (blot, dot or flame), microaneurysms, cotton wool spots, hard exudates. Malignant: moderate signs plus optic disc swelling. Moderate and malignant changes carry higher cardiovascular risk.

goDeeper.heading: What to do
goDeeper.body: Mild signs: advise the patient to have their BP checked by their GP. Moderate signs: refer to the GP more promptly, ideally with a BP reading. Signs of malignant hypertension (disc swelling, widespread haemorrhages/exudates) with very high BP: same-day referral. Follow local guidance and record what you advised.

topics.summary: PC-lab cases give you a patient's history and a set of results to interpret. Work systematically: check the data makes sense, compare eyes and visits, decide what's abnormal, link the findings into a diagnosis, then decide management.

goDeeper.heading: Visual field reliability
goDeeper.body: Before reading any defect, look at fixation losses, false positives and false negatives. High false positives (trigger-happy patient) make fields look better than they are; high false negatives can mimic defects. Commonly used cut-offs (e.g. false positives above about 15% with SITA) mark a test as unreliable — check the values your module uses. Repeat unreliable fields.

goDeeper.heading: Field indices
goDeeper.body: Mean deviation (MD): overall depression compared with age-matched normals (more negative = worse). Pattern standard deviation (PSD): how irregular the loss is (higher = more localised defects). Glaucoma hemifield test (GHT) compares superior and inferior field: 'outside normal limits' is suspicious. Look at the pattern deviation plot to see localised loss beyond general depression (e.g. cataract).

goDeeper.heading: Structuring your answer
goDeeper.body: 1) Summary of the key abnormal findings. 2) Most likely diagnosis and why. 3) Differentials and what rules them out. 4) Management: what you'd do, who you'd refer to and how urgently. 5) What you'd tell the patient. This structure works for almost every case.

topics.title: Referral urgency and writing referrals
topics.summary: Choosing the right urgency and writing a clear referral gets the patient seen by the right person at the right time. The College of Optometrists' Clinical Management Guidelines give urgency for most conditions; follow local pathways for where to send it.
keyPoints: Urgency categories (College CMGs) include emergency (same day), urgent (within about a week) and routine — check the exact definitions you're taught.
Emergency examples: retinal detachment, acute angle closure, suspected GCA, microbial keratitis, chemical injury (irrigate first), papilloedema.
Urgent examples: suspected wet AMD (via fast-track pathway), anterior uveitis (often same/next day), new unexplained field defects.
Routine examples: cataract affecting lifestyle, suspected COAG/OHT, stable chronic conditions.
Where to: eye casualty, hospital eye service via the local pathway, GP, or community schemes — depends on the condition and local services.
Referral letter contents: patient details, reason and urgency, history, relevant findings with numbers (VA, IOP, fields), what you've told the patient, your details and signature.
Tell the patient why, how urgently, and what to do if things get worse; record the referral.
examTraps: Under-calling urgency for GCA or retinal detachment.
Writing vague letters ('?glaucoma, please see').
Not telling the patient what to expect or what to do if symptoms worsen.

topics.title: The non-traumatic red eye
topics.summary: Sorting a red eye by history and a few signs: one eye or both, pain, photophobia, vision, discharge, pupil, cornea and anterior chamber. From the week 3 tutorial tables.
keyPoints: Unilateral red eye: think infection, acute glaucoma or iritis. Bilateral: conjunctivitis is more likely.
Conjunctivitis: viral is watery with cold symptoms and follicles; allergic is watery and itchy with puffy lids and papillae; bacterial is mucoid and crusty with lids stuck together.
Papillae: raised, red, central vessel, on the palpebral conjunctiva (allergy, bacteria, contact lenses). Follicles: pale domes with vessels around them, lower fornix (viral).

Corneal ulcer: pain, photophobia, watering and reduced VA with staining and an infiltrate. Contact lens wear and smoking point to infection; systemic illness such as rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis or inflammatory bowel disease points to a non-infectious cause.
Episcleritis: mild pain, VA normal, vessels move over the sclera. Scleritis: moderate to severe pain, VA reduced, vessels do not move, with intraocular inflammation.
Endophthalmitis: sudden painful red eye with cells, flare and hypopyon.

topics.title: Lids and orbit: lagophthalmos and proptosis
topics.summary: Incomplete lid closure and a bulging eye, from the week 4 tutorials: the causes to tell apart, the tests that matter, and how urgent each one is.
keyPoints: For lagophthalmos the needed tests are history, VA, cover test, motility and external examination; pupils, refraction, internal examination and IOP aren't needed.
Ectropion: urgent (2 weeks) if the cornea stains; routine if the cornea is normal.
Myasthenia gravis: intermittent binocular diplopia that varies with gaze, fatigable ptosis worse on sustained upgaze, lagophthalmos and surface staining.

Carotid-cavernous fistula: abnormal artery-to-cavernous-sinus connection (trauma or spontaneous, e.g. Ehlers-Danlos). Bruit, pulsating proptosis, brick-red vessels, chemosis, cranial nerve palsies; can cause angle-closure glaucoma or optic neuropathy.

Orbital cellulitis: infection spreading from sinuses, teeth or ears; sudden unilateral proptosis, lid oedema and redness, painful restricted movement, diplopia, RAPD. Can spread to the brain or cavernous sinus.
Thyroid eye disease: expansion of orbital fat and connective tissue, lid retraction, lagophthalmos, proptosis and incomitant deviation; red, staining eye when active, white when chronic.
examTraps: Forgetting that pinhole failing to improve VA rules out uncorrected refractive error.

Sixth nerve palsy: sudden horizontal diplopia worse in the affected direction, esotropia, limited abduction.
Fourth nerve palsy: vertical or oblique diplopia, hypertropia, head tilted towards the opposite shoulder.
Third nerve palsy: oblique diplopia, exotropia and hypotropia, limited adduction, elevation and depression, possibly ptosis and a poorly reacting dilated pupil.
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: poor adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye; linked to multiple sclerosis.
Decompensated phoria: intermittent diplopia worse when tired; the cover test shows poor recovery or breakdown to a tropia; everything else normal.
In the tutorial, palsies and gaze palsy come with swollen discs, which changes urgency and whether dilation is safe.
examTraps: Missing that diplopia varies with gaze direction: that points to a palsy, not a decompensated phoria.
Dilating without thinking about whether it's safe in a patient with a possible neurological problem.

topics.title: Visual field loss: causes and urgency
topics.summary: When a patient reports losing part of their vision, the history, IOP, fundus and field pattern separate retinal, optic nerve and brain causes, and set the urgency. From the week 9 tutorial.
keyPoints: Retinal detachment: vision lost like a curtain, IOP under 10 mmHg, tobacco dust (Shafer's sign), pale elevated retina. Macula-on vs macula-off changes urgency.
Acute optic neuropathy: sudden blur and unusual headaches with a hyperaemic, swollen disc. Progressive forms are gradual, with a swollen or a pale disc.
Wet AMD: sudden one-eyed blur with drusen, haemorrhage, grey-green membrane, exudates and oedema. Dry AMD: routine referral for low vision help if the patient wants it.
Glaucoma: gradual, painless, repeatable field loss that respects the horizontal midline.
Brain disease: transient bilateral blur, headaches worse lying down, flashes, neurological symptoms, swollen discs, and homonymous loss respecting the vertical midline.
TIA: seconds of blur or sparkling lights with neurological symptoms (vertigo, weakness, numbness); everything else normal.
examTraps: Missing low IOP as a clue to retinal detachment.
Giving a single urgency for conditions where it depends on the findings (e.g. macula on or off, how recent wet AMD is).
